THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT

(1871) AMENDMENT BILL.

Mn. HARRISON is not correct when he
says—" The evils of this Act have led to
attempts to repeal it, or to modify it." No
attempt to repeal or modify the Act has yet
been made, other than the Bill now before the
House of Commons," backed" by Mr. VERNoIi
HARCOURT', MT. HENRY JAMES, 'Mr. A. J.
MUNDELLA, Mr. GEORGE DIXoN, and Mr.
GEORGE MELLY. The history of the Bill will
be given at the proper time and in the proper
place; meanwhile we acknowledge its pa.
rentage, and own it as our Bill.
Mr. IlAnnisort is quits right in supposing
that we have satisfied ourselves that this is all
we oan get from this House of Commons; and
I am glad that Mr. HARRISON does not mean to
"throw any doubt on the public spirit and
prudence of those (not politicians) who promote
the Bill." Mr. ilLuntsol. says—" It is ob-
viously, from their point of view, well in-
tended." I am glad to Ifnd that it is obviously
so from Mr. HannisoN'a standpoint.

. ,
As to the 13111 not, being a solution
of the queitiOn, that
,of course entirely
depends upon the intended Meaning of the
,ex-
pression. Possibly we entirely agree with Mr.
HARRII3OII. I know not Mr.'
,HARRIFION'S
meaning when he speaks about a show of
support from. working Men's representatives,"
neither do I know on what authority lie speaks
when he adds—" I know that the workmen, as
a body, cannot assent to anything of the
kind." The wish possibly is father ,to the
thuught, but the data upon which it is stated
I know not.

How, and in what way, could the fact of
our having promoted this Bill stultify our
oppo,sition to al° Combination Laws, or to the
Act of last year? I certainly see it not, and
yet I stood as one of the most uncompromis-
ing to the entire Bill of last session. But let

us ey,4llllille the charges of Mr. HARRIS' ON.
Ile asserts that" The new Bill re-imposes and
repeats every one of the obnoxious features of
the Act of 1871, with the single exception
that it omits the penalty on watching and
besetting." Let Mr. IllaßrsoN point out to
us which of the prosecutions under the Act
could have been sustained under the present
Bill.
The mere re-nrrangement of the clauses
and subsections', so we are informed by high
legal authority, tends to prevent confusion,
alai with it also some of the uujust deoisious

of magistrates from want of proper defini-
tions.
Mr. HARMON makes. this important ad-
mission : " That this latter clause, watching
and besetting, is the one most obviously unjust
in the late Act." How the late Act? Unfor-
tunately for us, it is the *sent ACV. Wells, our
object has been to get rid of the one practical
blot in the Act of last session, because expense.
and suffering has been the result of that clause
It can scarcely be said that "there is a penalty
for a new crime introduced," inasmuch £lB the
whole scheme of re-arrangement was to pre-
vent the creation of crimes by magisterial
law.

Mr. HARRISON seems to leave the position
of a friendly critic for that of the special
pleader in the last paragraph of his article, for.
what purpose does not appear. The Bill 'ivas
not promoted by the House of Commons, but
by the Committee, and our motive
for countenancing It was for the Purpose
of relieving the workman from the terror
of existing law. It is an attempt to
take the sting out of the Act of 1871,
and it is neither opposed to the protest
of last year, nor to the condemnation of the
Nottingham Conference. And, as an amend-
ment, we still feel that, if it became law, so
much the better for the workman than the
present Act.

• Mr. Hatursorr says, "it has not had the
sanction of thosp•who have advised the, work.=
men-in the matter:" I beg leave to say that
Mr. HAnitTiorr had a proof copy Sent
to hint ' soon 'as I could get it
from the printers, before even it was sent
to Mr. VERNON HAECOnT, so that' it might
receive either his emendation or advice:
But he never sent me one word in reference
thereto. This concluding sentence of Mr.
HkitRIBON is quite 'gratuitous ---" 'Working
m.en
,and their representatives can give this
measure no eountenance Without being false
to all they have 'hitherto agreed, and to the
true interests of free labour." Mr. HAunrspN
might have sent his adviee direct to ilie"Coin-
mittee, without endeavouring to stir up strife,
especially as the Bill has never been printed
by the House with the clause complained of
in it. Mr. HARRI4ON was not the first to
express fear of that sub- section.
Our past life in the labour, and other
naovements, is the best answer to insinuation of
falseness to the interest's of our class, and we
feel perfectly assured by our conscience that
our attempt to amend the law has been an
honest one, and we have yet to learn that it
will not be for the benefit of our class.

It is not the first time that Professor
BEESLY has tried his hand at bespattering
mud, and we fear not but that its splashes
will rebound on the person of the thrower. The
Professor need not be astonished that the
"Parliamentary Committee" have, under
efficient legal advise, promoted the said Bill.
Men who strive honeStly to do their duty need
not be ashamed of their handicraft. I should
be quite prepared to rest on the Bill as it is,
unless my interpretation of its wording differ,
materially from that of others.
The clause in dispute -did not escape our
• notice, for it caused uS kie veal special inter.
views for the purpose of trying to make it
as . little open to objection as possible.
I never ceased to feel anxiety on
the . subject until it was ' withdrawn.

•
Our pffarts were directed to the picketing clause
together with the endeavour to strip the Bill
of the ambiguity previously complained of.
As to the word." intimidate," it occurs in this
Bill in such a manner, as we are advised, not
so easily to be misconstrued as in the Act—
not so much by new words as by re-arrange-
Ment.
When Professor B EMT is appointed At-
torney-General for 'trades societies, it will, be
the duty of committees to consult him on all
such technical points as the constructien of
Acts of Parliament, without even so much as
oxPressing an opinion on the choice so made.
But this committee never once hinted to me
that it was my duty to consult the Professor,
who, not long since, could libel the whole
class of trades unions officers and leaders, as
was done by him in'this paper. *
As to
,Mr. flErtnY Cuomrrox-, I consulted
him at every step taken up to the very day on
which he left London for the Continent. I,
moreover, seii a prpof copy of ,the proposed
Bill to Mr. MAROOrr. before it was given to
Mr. VEIIN ON Iliacorrur for the Parliamentary
printers, but I never reeeived one line from
him in acknowledgment thereof.

We have no desire to waste our time scowling
at the moon, and therefore we agreed to try
and, amend a bad law, which oppresses our
working trades unionists, ()lien while we may
object to the very principle of the law itself.
_

The whole history of the Bill will be given
to the Congress, by whom we are appointed,
who are our constituents, and by their verdict
we shall be content to abide. If the Professor
can undertake to get through Parliament
another and a better Bill, I will gladly resign
my secretaryship into his hands.

The learned Professor has learnt much from

the very men at whom ha now snarls, and if
he will only dispense with the notion that he
is the positive high priest of:labour, all others
notwithstanding, ho may yet ,learn mote. But,_
it is the " Parliamentary: 'pernioittee " :that
the ill tempered Profetieer trie!i'to hit, rather
than the Pill. Let those who cavil show us a
more exeellopt way. 'Let them tell us how to,
get through Parliament a Bill which Will pre-
vent the prosecutions which we recently pub-
lished as occurring under this Act, and we
will gladly adopt their method, if it commend
itself for the probability of its success.

We desire to remove both the sentimental
and the practical grievapoe,
.but ifl)oth cannot
be got rid of at the same time, let us bear the
former to get rid of the latter. When the

agitation for repealing the remnants of the
old Combination LOMB N9.s going on, and the Bill
was under debate, I attended a meeting at Starn-
ford-street at which Professor BIcSLY was pre-
sent; but Mr.,V. M. LUDLOW and myself wore the
only two who took the strong ground that we
had better go against all legislation other than
repeal, and simplify the permanent enactment
of the temporary law for the protection of
trades unions' funds.
At the deputation to Mr. Bitrcz in 1871,

one spoke so pointedly against the tendency
of the Government Bill as I
.did, and I Wiiti
taken to task by 501110 of our middle.class
advisers "lest I should endaeger the Bill."
Even now, our good and old 'hind, TUOMAS
UUGUES, refuses to take any part for the
purpose of repealing the present law, ana
even thinks our oppo4ition to it, or attempt
to modify it, a mistake.
, Mr. NILqi,DELL.A. Arid Mr. IL. 8. ANTluctia Ups

been with us iu all our discussions during
,the
'construction and drsughting of the Bill.
Mr. RATIIBONE would have brought in a Bill
to repeal simply the words of the Lords'
4n3endment, but then the doubtful construc-
tion of the Act remained.. Reconstruction
seemed the easiest and best way; hence our
countenance thereof.

One thing I must add in conclusion, namely
that I have always opposed all legislation on
the subject, excepting a repeal of the remnant
of the old Combination Laws; but we were
always advised by our middle-class friends
that some further legislation was necessary,
and I with others reluctantly consented.
To this we owe the present law, and this
attempt to amend it. We are content to
leave our entire Conduct in this matter to the
members of the next Trades Congrefrs, to
whom we shall givo every information as to
our work.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT
ACT. •

IN the introductory remarks to the hill, which
professes to be a Bill to amend the provi-
ideas of the, Criminal Law Amendment Act,
1871," it is stated that "the Bill is prepared
by the Committee" which was elected as the
Parliamentary Cemmittee by the Trades.Cou:-
gress. Now, if this Bill has been prepared by,
the Committee, it has altogether exceeded its
functions, as the Committee bad no authority:
whatever to prepare any such Bill. . Bat
,I am,
informed :that some of the principal member
of this Parliamentary Committee were never
consulted about this Bill, nor, in fact, ever
Informed. of, or invited. to attend, any Com-,
inittee meeting upon ther,eubject,
~ Now the
Trades Congress at Nottingham pronounced a
very decid.ed opinion, and. gave a unanimous
vote upon the resolution, which was submitted
for its approval and
,adoption, and. which I
here reproduce in proof of the determination
of that Congress to go for the total repeal of
the Act..
The resolution is to the following effect
:-
"That this Congress is of opinion that the
Criminal Law Amendment Act is unjust and
exceptional in chaise*, :1114 oPpreiseiie in its
application to the personal. freedom of, the
working claasee of the , United, Kingdom ;
therefore this Congress pledgee, itself to use
every legal means to secure the repeal of the
Act." Now it is hard to believe that the
Committee appointed by. the Congress would
prepare such a miserable abortion of a
Bill as the one issued. in their names,
particularly as some of them spoke strongly
in favour of passing that resolution by the
Congress. If those who were instrumental in
passing this Act, or the qovernment who
acoepted the Lords' amendments, are
.begin-
ning to get ashamed of their handiwork, and.
think proper to suggest or propose any imead-
•
ment to, the Act,, by all moans let it have due
attention and consideration. But surely it is
not the business of any of tho trades delegates,
.mueli lees the Parliamentary Committee, who
are pledged to. its' repeal, to begin to tinker
, and amend this Act? Their duty, and that
of the whole body of trades unionists through-
out the 'United Kingdom, is clearly to insist
upon its total repeal. But, perhaps, it may
be said the present Parliament will not repeal
the Criminal Law Amendment Act. Well,
what of that He must be a very short-
'sighted politician who expects a majority of
the present, Parliament to either repeal that
Act, pass a Mines Regulation Bill, a Payment
of Wages Bill, or a Truck. Act, in the shape
that any of these measures ought to be passed.
But what the working men have to do is to
force these questions upon the attention of
successive Parliaments until they become sa-
tisfactory and, aoceptable to them, and give
that protection and eeou.rity they have a right
to expect. manner, instead of accept.;
.ing any miserable compromise as being satis-
faotpry, they mut iusist upon the total repeal
of the .C4lnit4ll Law. Auleuipent 4.efi •gnd en-,

&savour to get as many of the leading working
men into the next Parliament as possible, to
assist in doing this. Mr. KA.NE, of Darlington,
proposed a resolution, which was carried
unanimously, at the Trades' Congress,
that the repeal of this Act should be a
test to all candidates at the next election,
and he has nobly set the example himself by
administering a sound castigation to some of
the north country ALP.'s who not only voted
for this Act but are also supporters of the
Truck system. And I see the men of Leeds
are about to hold a demonstration against this
Act, and other towns are also protesting against
it. The working men may rely upon it, they
will have a hard battle to fight before they get
rid of this most unjust and oppressive Act. It
is an easy matter to get an Act like this passed
rapidly through a Parliament of capitalists, but
it is a hard matter to get it repealed.
Whatever object the legal gentlemen in the
House of Commons may have in view in pro-
moting the so-called amended Bill, the
working men will make a serious mistake if
they give ,it 'any countenance or support.
But if, legal advice was required in drafting
any proposed amendment to this Act, one
would have supposed that such men as Mr.
FREDERICK HARRISON and Mr. HENRY
CROMPTON, who have rendered essential service
before in connection with this Act, would have
been applied to, instead of the very doubtful
assistance of Mr. VERNON HARCOURT and Mr.
HENRY JAMES. No doubt it may answer the
purpose of both these legal gentlemen to be
very patriotic after having played the
character. of MARPLOT3, in doing their utmost
to spoil the Ballot Bill, and take their revenge
upon the Government for being blind to their
superior abilities and claims to promotion. At
the same time, it is questionable whether they
will regain the respect they have lost by many
of their constituents, through their vagaries on
the Ballot Bill, by merely tinkering and pre-
tending to amend the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act.

I have repeatedly, requested the advoqates
of this Act to point out the necessity for passing
it, and I have never yet had that question
answered, I ought to know as much about
the virtues or vices, the faults or good qualities,
of working mon as any man living. I have
sprung from the workshop myself, and since I
have been engaged in another capacity, I have
had, thousands of .trades unionists
.under me,
in different , parts of the country, for the last
twenty-five years, I, never was the man to
pander to their prejudices or humour their follies,
but I have no hesitation in saying that I never
found any difficulty in dealing with them, if
they Were only treated in a fair, off-hand,
'straightforward manner. I am convinced
, that the common or ordinary statute law is
quite sufficient to deal with any unlawful act
committed by trades unionists or , others.
If an assault be committed that is very easily
dealt with, or if intimidation or threatening
language ,be proved against any , of them,
the necessary
tpunishment follows. If the
secretary run' away with any of the funds of
these societies' now that they are legal, and
the old Combination Laws arc abolished,
why he would be punished just the same as
the secretary of the Master Builders' Associa-
tion, or the secretary of the Institute of
Architects would be punished. Therefore,
there must be some other sinister and covert
motive in maintaining this Criminal Law
Amendment Act, and its object and intention
is not far to seek.

It is to be found in the fact that many of
the employers and capitalists are above all
things desirous of preventing pioketting when
any strike takes place or dispute arises—that,
in fact, it shall be rendered dangerous, and if
necessary, criminal fur any man on strike to
speak to or remonstrate with any of the men
which the masters have kidnapped. and put
into their places. The employer may bring
men under the most false pretences, and may
use the most unscrupulous means, short of
force, to keep them ; but if the men they hay
supplanted offer any remonstrance or attempt
to give any explanation, it is at their peril
,and risk, and within. the power of any scamp
betray them into the hands of the Philistines,
get them convicted of ",raolestation" or " be-
, setting with % view .to coerce,',' fuld
,Away they

thaws 7,
,1872,

go to prison, and the brand and stigma of
criminality is attached to them for the re:.-
minder of their days.
Now, if this be the proper way to treat the
great wealth-producing class in this country,
and they are content that it should remain se,
it is of small consequence to me beyond pro
-
clueing profound grief in my mind to behold
their servility. But better things than
may very fairly be expected of thern. No .
doubt the working men are greatly at fault in
sending a considerable number of the men to
Parliament they did at the last election. Let
them beware of this next time, and prepare,
without delay, to send as many as possible of
the best and most experienced men from their
own ranks to represent them in Parliament at -
the next election.

ALFRED A. WALTON.

MR. ODGER AND THE F/G.l RO.
Jr appears to me that Mr. ODOM is NAY
entitled to the apology which he requests at
the hands of the proprietors of .Egaro,
and that they have acted unwisely in adopting
the course which they propose to pursue.
There can be no doubt, as stated in the very
temperate letter written by his solicitors, that
the sole effect and purpose of the articles
published in that journal has been calcu-
lated to injure, if not to destroy, his personal
reputation, and it is unworthy of the pro-
prietors to refuse the apology which is posi-
tively called for by the circumstances of the
case. I do not see what other course can be
pursued, if this is refused, but to appeal to
another tribunal, and the parties offending
will simply have themselves to blame if the
verdict given is an adverse one. The pro-
minence given to an intended justification,
which appears in the issue of the 18th ult.,
shows that a considerable degree of importance
is attached to the charge that has been made ;
and I cannot help thinking that the writer of
that article, probably the author of the alleged
libel, feels keenly that he has placed himself
in a false position, and one from
which he would gladly withdraw, were It not •
that some antiquated notions of obstinaey
peculiar to the Tory party, and that portion
of the Press by which it is represented, prevented
him doing what would only be a graceful, not
to say a just act, of reparation.
I may state that I have the greatest respect
for the wit and intelligence that has been
displayed by the writers in this very amusing
journal; and there is no doubt that in many
cases the criticisms that have appeared from
time to time have been just and dignified—
not even excepting those for which the pro-
prietors have, as I consider, unjustly been
called to account. But I am by no-means
prepared, nor do I think , any right-ininded
man will be prepared, to endorse the some-
what libellous remarks that have been pub-
lished with reference to Mr. Doom who
seems to me to have a fair cause of complaint
against Mr. MonTrnEa, who, by-the-byo,
takes a great deal of pains to inform the
public that he is the proprietor of Figaro,
and who also, on the man-trap and spring-gun
principle, we suppose, seems very anxious to
drag before the publio the names of the very
eminent firm of solicitors that he has deputed
to act for him ; however, we have no doubt that
they are proportionately grateful for the
publicity thus so generously given.
But whilstl give full credit to the paper for the
talent that has been shown in what may be
fairly termed its literary department, I am by
no means disposed to praise that part which has
been devoted to the consideration of subjeot
of a political character. It is stated that the
conductors do not profess to be "purveyors of
journalistic treacle." I am not very dear as
to what is meant by this.strange assertion, but
I think that the readers of Figaro 101
agree with me, that a 'great deal of gross and
fulsome adulation has been bestowed
upon a certain distinguished individual
who has lately honoured this country by
making it his plaee of residence. By-the-
bye, what a splendid opportunity the ex
-
EMPEROR of the FRENCH has lost. Could
not some of his advisers have arranged that the
poor devils of Communists who were so un-
ceremoniously landed at Dover the other
day, should homo been sent en roar to LOU"

don, via Cirisleharst i) A little management
would have scoured their introduction to NA-
POLEON 111., and the spectacle of his playing
the Good Samaritan to a section of those
misguided men who had done their best to
drive him and his family from the throne,
could not fail to have a salutary effect upon
the minds of many who are now engaged in
their futile endeavours to overthrow 'consti-
tuted authorities. As we are likely, from all
accounts, to have many more deportations of
the same character, I commend this idea to
the consideration of his Imperial majesty.

A revenant.; nos moutons, There may or may
not be between Mr. OMER and the gentlemen
who write for Figaro, a wide and impassable
social gulf. At any rate, we have the assurance
of the Editor that such is the ease, and I, for
one, am not going out of my way to contradict
the assertion ; but it should be borne in mind
that gentlemanly feeling is not shown by the im-
putation of motives which have no existence but
in the overstrained imaginations of partial
writers. One thing Ido object to, that is, that
Mr. ODGER or his advisers have not flown at
higher game. Surely the abuse of Republi-
canism has not been confined to Figaro.
Journals of a very much higher standing
have, from time to time, contained articles
much more abusive, if not more libellous, than
that which it is now sought to make the
ground of an action. Fair play is prized
amongst working men as much as it
is amongst the superior classes. I think
that if any wrong has been offered to Mr.
ODGER—IInd I am by no means sure that the
utterances of several high class journals have
not eonstituted an injustice, there are many
who believe in him as being other than a noisy
agitator who would have assisted him to secure
reparation.
.The ill-advised article in the Figaro that
appears in reply to the communication of his
solicitors renders anything like a compromise
difficult; and, if it has been decided to have
the question tried, we hope the complainant
will have fair play. Doubtless, there are men of
peculiarly constituted minds who derive a
certain amount of satisfaction from traducing
the character of those with whose opinions
they do net agree; but it will have a whole-
some effect on some of these gentlemen if it is
shewn that they cannot do so with im-
punity.
In the event of a subscription being raised
to procure proper counsel, I shall be happy to
back my opinion by contributing to the same.
W. H. Dlvrs.

Iv you will kindly allow me space in your
columns to inform Dr. SANDWITTC that where
your printer printed "the old common days,"
I had written" the old Comorn days," it may
perhaps throw some light on that passage in
my letter which he finds so "obscure."
For the rest, it would be idle to continuo
the contro foray with Dr. SAYDWITII, because
it is evident that he has not read the whole of
my letter, or he does not believe what I say;
and, in either case, it would be useless for me
to address him again. I told him that the
Shield, the organ of our Association, had
always pleaded "for the admission of all suf-
ferers from venereal disease, into all our hos-
pitals." Nevertheless, he "fears that the
coffers of the National Association for. the
Repeal, &c., are largely helped" by those who
"forbid the medical officers of the hospitals
throughout the country to relieve poor suf-
fering human beings afflicted with this fell
disorder." This, it he believed my assertion,
would be to suppose a class of monied lunatics,
who fill our coffers in order to enable us to
preach what they (3 forbid" shall be done. I
asked him to point out where he found, not
merely the words he placed iu inverted
commas (as typical of our sentiments), but
any words to the same eject in any publication
of ours. Upon this point he is silent, and I
cannot help suspecting that he has not read
any of our writings, and that he is somewhat
in the position of the schoolboy who shouted
" Bogie" without looking round, merely
because the other lads shouted Bogie, and
startled him. lie thinks "this is scarcely the
occasion upon which ho can Accept my inyita-

tion to give his ideas of the nature of the
CREATOR." But finite beings can only form
their idea of the CREATOR from His works, and
to tell us what are the " imperious demands
of human nature," is implicitly to tell us
what the CREATOR is who gave that nature to
His creatures. Believing, as I do, in. a GOD
who is the Father of the human race, I believe
that all the laws of nature are just and
paternal; that our one sole duty is to
seek to know, in order that we may in-
telligently obey those laws, and that all
the temporary evil and suffering in the world
results from our ignorance or neglect of them.
Therefore, when a "demand ", is made by
one-half of the human race which cannot be
supplied without causing the 'physical and

articles.text:
GOVERNMENT JUSTIGE AND
ECONOMY.

A TITLE without the ways and means of
supporting it soon falls into liquidation. So
it is with our supposed " Liberal " Govern-
ment. When the people of this country placed
the power of government in the hands of the
present Ministers, they also placed with it their
confidence, fancying that at last they should
have a Government that represented the voice
of the nation. But alas! their hopes were
doomed to disappointment. Even the far-famed
orator, and once popular personage, Mr.
GLADSTONE, has blighted our hopes and expec-
tations, and we find that he is no more the
friend of the working ()lasses than his financial
friend, Mr. Chancellor LowE, who, it is said,
would abolish a part of the Income Tax rather
than carry out the excellent plan of Mr. Joux
Bitiowr, and provide us with a free break-
fast-table." The man of matches and
whiggistu will, no doubt, on the first oppor-
tunity, further reduce the Income Tax to gain
the applause of his own .particular class, and
the aristocratic noodles that offer their friend-
ship in exchange for robbing the poor of their
rights.
That this country's ,money is wasted away
in a disgraceful manner, is an undoubted fact;
aria that every high nominal official under
Government is paid largo and preposterous
salaries—for being " gentlemen's" sons—
whilst they that du all the work are offered a
miserable pittance for their long and laborious
work, is a well-known and disgraceful cireutn-
stance.
That the working classes are dissatisfied
with such a Government is no wonder; and
that its downfall is certain is no surprise even
to those that support it and help to pack up
buch an oratorical heap of blunders.
Wished-fur inquiries into the roots of
" worldly evil," is stormed and nintilated by
the censuring sneers of the person that was
placed in his present position, by the interesters
and desirers of that particular inquiry. Praised
and applauded by the saplings and branches
of that root of worldly evil, their power has
only survived that its downfall may be more
sure and humiliating than ever.
It appears that the country's money can-
not be squandered fast enough; that its
channel of disappearance is not wide enough,
but that they must now prosecute the
" claimant " to the Tiehborne estates, and
allow a man to conduct the case, whose
language has not yet been proved either
rhetorical, truthful, or
,just; awl who at least
may lay claim to the disgust and contempt of
a majority of the populatioa of Great Britain.

It might not be out of place here to endorse
the words expressed by a certain well-known
and, respected. gentleman, who said that it
was a rare occurrence for the voice of the
British nation to be incorrect in passing an
opinion.
Once on a tune we had imaginary glimpses
Of what we thought to be a true Liberal
Government, but we find that it was but a
chimera of whriit it should be, brightly gilded
and overcast by the rhetorical language of
eloquent prepossessing orators.
The beautiful speeches of Mr. GLADSTONE
at times would seera to half transpose the
public mind, and lead them to fancy ,that
such remarkable
.eloquence could never leave
the lips of aught but an excellent gentleman
that was sincere and determined, to bo true to
a nation's trust. But, like dreamers of a bye..
gone age, we awaken to observe the true state
of affairs and see treaties mis-managed ; our
ships sinking beneath the waves; and our
money squandered in prosecutions, which are
directly in opposition to justice and the voice
of the nation. When all these things rise up
before us, and many others that have far from
sunk into oblivion, and we still bear the
rhetorical eloquenoe of our Prime Minister,
we are compelled to pronounce it vox et preeterea
nihil ("sound and nothing more.")

EARL RUSSELL'S MOTION.

Eau RUSSELL has at last had his say
about the Alabama Claims. The speech will
be remembered for the power as well as the
weakness which it showed in harmony with
the efforts of the same speaker in younger
years. In short, he does net like arbitration
in such matters, and therefore he likes neither
the Treaty of VTashington nor the Tribunal
of Geneva. Instead of showing cause against
the Supplementary Article, he denounced the
whole concern, contending that the Treaty
excluded the claims, yet condemning the
Commissioners for not seeing that they were
excluded, Practically he wants us to repeat
our refusal to listen to such demands, after
the American Government has really with -
drawn them, and to censure our own Govern-
ment whfle OAT are doing all they on, uador

JtiiM 7'L

the deepest sense of responiibility, to conduct
negoeiations to the point of a satisfactory
settlement.

Lord DERBY endeavoured to reduce the
question to oneof mode and of manner, rather
than of substance; but it did not suit the
Government to let it go from the ground cm
which Earl RUSSELL'S stronger arraignmente.
had placed it. Lord au,rsetrar's tone- was
tumidly anti-American, and was answered by
by Lord Rtrox in a way that may soothe our
irritated kinsmen without having committed
himself. On the part of the Government the
motion and the speech in its support were
regarded as a censure on themselves and a
menace to the negociations. Lord KruntatvEY
addressed himself to those parts of the question
which have an aspect towards his Depart-
ment. The substantial defence of Ministers
was lathe hands of Lord Gakrivius, who,
though the Lord CHANCELLOR has yet to
reply to the criticisms of Lord CAIRNS and
sarcasms of Lord WESTBURY, may be regarded
as having disposed of matter. Rising with;
the occasion, he became not simply argumen-
tative and discriminatory, but warmly • and
powerfully eloquent. Contrasting the decant
tone of Earl RUSSELL with the calmness of
Lord DERBY, and calling attention to the
"Statesmanlike reticence" of Mr. Disiuifl
opposition to the mischievous talkativeness of
members of the Opposition, not so wise or So
moderate, he concluded with answering the
noble mover's instigation to greater pluck by
maintaining that trite courage is shown in
giving up not one jot of what the dignity and
honour of the country demands; but, on the
other hand, in avoiding all irritating expres-
sions towards foreign Powers.

articles.title: OPEN POINT BETWEEN ENGLAND AND AMERICA.
articles.text:
THE OPEN POINT BETWEEN ENGLAND
AND AMERICA.

IT is no uncommon thing for men to flatter
themselves that a thing fairly done by another
man could have been as well or better done by
themselves. But, when a man or a number of
men meet with difficulties in the way of their
attempts, and are even obliged to confess
themselves baffled and defeated, a multitude
are ready to spring up and show how easily
they could have managed the matter. The
Alabama difficulty has brought about displays
of this kind. Both Houses of Parliament
contain quite a number of men who, had they
been in the places of Mr. GLapirrozaf and
Earl GILUIVILLE, would have mado nothing of
it. Not, however, that either of the Ministers
acknowledges himself beaten. Leairing Earl
RussELL in one House and Lord Burr in the
other to make what they can. of it, we will
carefully consider what the PRIME MINISTER
tells us, and see whether by any admission or
implication of his, it is altogether a hopeless
case.

There is evidently a difference of view
between the American Government and our
own, though its precise nature and extent do
not yet transpire. According to President
GRANT, a simple exchange of notes between
the two would have warranted him in. not
pressing for payment of the indirect claims.
But these claims would not be aheo;
lutely witlidrawii without the 0011011 Y•
rem of the American Senate. Whigs led to
the conception and proposal of the Supple-
mentary Article. It was prepared by tha
QtrzEs's advisers, in conjunction with, not '
only the ATTORNEY and SOLICITOR.GENNTIA,T,O
but also the LORD CHANCELLOR and Sir
ROUNDELL PALMER. Although Lord CAIRNS
and. Lord WESULTRY made little of this strong
consultation, most people will be of opinion
that, outside the Administration, a better,
choice could not have been exercised than in
taking the advice of the man whom nothing
but high principle has kept off the Woolsack lit
this Cabinet; and who, as Mr. GLADSTONE
reminded us, accepted the office of counsel to
Government in the pending Arbitration. nlO
possible that a whole people may think lesm
than satisfactory that which to the first legal
knowledge and mammon has commended itself
as equal to the purpose, that purpose being, in
this case, the positive exclusion of sone*"
pential claims.

,
But what is of first importance is, the ft"
. _
agreement of the two Powers in the re"
instrument and in its appendix, Noir, We-

have Mr. GLA.DBTOITEN clear authority for the
statement, that negotiations remain incomplete
'from no known or supposed desircion the part
Of the Government in Washington to "pro-
cure a weakening, a dilution of the covenant,"
the covenant, that is, which would exclude
the claims in question. Ito also distinctly
'states, that, between them and us, there exists
-4‘ no difference whatever as to either the letter
or the spirit of that part of the stipulations."
The American authorities, in short, accept
without hesitation or reserve the view that the
article as it stands shuts out the claims;
which, if adopted, will therefore cease to be.

The unfinished discussion, we are informed
by the Pnitsran, turns wholly and solely upon.
"prospective engagements." In spirit, both
'Governments declare an equal willingness to
put an end for the future to the notion of con-
sequential claims founded upon violations of
neutrality in time of war. The single question
remaining open is, in what precise form of
words this shall be expressed. Hence the re-
port which reaches us from Washington, that
if the British Ambassador there be authorised
to sign the Supplementary Article in the form
given to it by the American Senate, Presi-
dent GRANT will consent to a new joiut com-
mission for the purpose of, arranging a special
Treaty defining the rights of neutrals with
relation to what are styled consequential
damages. In the meantime, by a week's pro-
longation of its session, Congress has afforded
to the Senate an opportunity, " has
opened a door," through which a full
and final settlement may more immediately
be reached: not merely more immediately,
but, as Mr. GLA.DSTONE seems to hope and
believe, in consistency with the due opening
of the Conference of Arbitration in Geneva.
If words have meaning and statesmen
probity, Mr. GLADSTONE and his colleagues
have anticipated Mr. OSBORNE'S call upon them
to insist that "the indirect claims be fully,
fairly, and at once withdrawn." On a review
of his statement we find that the premature
publication of official papers was due, not to
the American Government, but to the "enter-
prise" of the press. Then, as to the
words "for the future," supposed by some to
be applicable to the engagement not to make
any claim at Geneva, these words are applicable
only to the last clause but one; and the
engagement of the PRESIDENT, supposed to be
undertaken in virtue and in consideration of
what has. preceded, is not to be limited by any
such application as these words might appear
to imply; that is, so far as regards the opinion
of the Government and of those upon whom
they rely for legal guidance as to the force of
terms and expressions in this matter. With
respect, however, to that point, our Govern-
ment have not the slightest reason
to believe, that there is any differ-
ence of construction upon the two
sides. Telegraphic messages are far loss full
than oommunioations by pos.t. Explanations
are rarely offered. until some challenge makes
it necessary, and no challenge whatever in-
dicating difference of opinion has taken place.
As to the transition from the proposal first
made to proceed by interchange of notes to
that other method, the whole treaty-making
power of the United States, which includes
the Senate as well as the Government, the
state of the case was this. President GRANT
held the Indirect Claims strictly admissible
under the Treaty as a formal document im-
posing-pertain obligations. Although, there-
fore, he conceived himself perfectly warranted
by interchange of notes in agreeing not to
prose for compensation, yet he did not oonceive
itlay within his discretion to withdraw those
claims. The word "withdrawal" may be open,
quite irrespective of feeling with regard, to
technical discussion, because in the Treaty
the claims exist. When people express a
desire that they should be withdrawn, they
wish to be secured that no further proceeding
tending to a practical solution, whether in the
shape of money, or of the expression of
opinion, or in any other shape, should be open
to be taken upon them. This, the PRESIDENT
considered, could only be done by the whole
treaty-making power, and he expressed the
desire, that, instead of notes, the two Govern-
ments should proceed by a Supplementary
krtiole, under which, for MU) OOMCIOUt COU•

sideration, the United States might declare
they would make no claim for such losses, and
the arbitrators would be prevented from enter-
taining the claims. That, says the Pittman,
is our view of the case ; and our belief is, that
that is the sense the American Government
places upon the ultimate clause of the Supple-
mentary Article. That, too, is the view made
known to the representative of the United States
at this Court, and which has received his
concurrence. There has been aprevading impres-
sion of an carton thepart of the United States to
procure a weakening, a dilution of the covenant,
whereby the PRESIDENT is supposed to under-
take that he will make no claim in respect of
the indirect losses before the arbitrators at
Geneva. That is not so. No such attempt
whatever has been made, and there is no
difference whatever between the two Govern-
ments as to the letter of the stipulation, or, as
far as Mr. GLADSTONE knows, as to its spirit
Or construction. The subject of communica-
tions has been entirely different. It has
related to that portion of the Article which
has not received the same critical attention as
the more immediately operative words, but
which, notwithstanding, it was a duty, as it
refers to an obligation to be carried into effect,
to weigh and canvass with the utmost minute-
ness.. In fact, the remaining question is
altogether prospective. As to making known
the amendments proposed by the Senate, our
Government have come to the conclusion that
it would not be consistent with due respect to
the Senata and Government of the United
States that they should be produced. There
is no difference, however, existing, or likely to
exist, in reference to the indirect claims, pre-
suming an understanding with regard to
prospective engagements, which, it is obvious,
is a very nice matter to express in words.

articles.title: BALLOT BILL AND THE HYPOCRISY OF PARLIAMENT.
articles.text:
THE BALLOT BILL AND THE HYPO-
CRISY OF PARLIAMENT.

IT is very much to be desired that the Ballot
Bill was somehow or other got out of the way.
A considerable section of the Liberal party,
whilst professing a respect for it, did what
they could to mutilate it; whilst the Conser-
vatives, notwithstanding their frequently ex-
pressed opinion that it would tell in their
favour as a party, did their best to dofeat it.
If the Lords pass it as it is, the people will
receive it without gratitude, and without
much hope as to its beneficial operation.
There never was a measure before Parliament
that caused so much dishonest talk, or which
had so direct a tendency to lower the reputa-
tion of the House of Commons for sincerity of
speech and singleness of purpose.
The history of our representation furnishes
a curious illustration to the speeches of our
legislators on this subject. That last Galway
election shining out as a marvellously-executed
tail-piece, glowing all over with life and
character. Who could think after snob an
exposure of replying seriously to the NEWDE-
GATES, the SILITTLS, the BENTINCRS, the
NORTRCOTES, and others who at the last
moment raised the old " unEnglish " croak?
These men know that the English people are
long suffering and patient. They know, or
they ought to know, that previous to 1832 this
same kind of dishonest nonsense was talked
for the purpose of preventing the change's then
made. Multitudes of honest English gentle-
men, like those
_whose sense of independence
makes them detest the Ballot, were quietly
filling their pockets and enriching their families
at the expense of the nation:; whilst they were,
at the same time, mouthing disgusting non-
sense about English honour, the sacredness of
the English constitution, and the inestimable
value of English liberty.
_ _

They had then the representation of the
country in their hands dirootly, unmistakably.
Aldborough, with its throe houses rated at .£lO
and upwards, and two members, Beerlaston
with its one rated house and its two members.
Bossiney with its one house above £lO, and
two members. About a score of little pocket
boroughs, which, for thirty years before the
passing of the Reform Bill of 1832, had re-
turned two members each on nomination,
without a contest. These and many other
were merely conduit pipes through which
publie plunder passed into the posses-

sion of a number of "fine old English
gentlemen" who were very respectable
and who grew fat on the spoil
They did the thing openly. They and their
highly-born sons ',had [their hands out in all
directions whenever anything was to be got by
the asking or taking, all the time singing
patriotic songs and whistling national tunes
about greatness, and honour, and glory. And
in their zeal for things as they were they
sneered at, scoffed, and flouted all who pro-
tested against the barefaced system of plunder
by which they grew rich.

What they had by direct hold of represen-
tative influence their descendants enjoy in-
directly.
,They could send orders to the con-
stituencies to return their nominees. The
present men have to adopt a different plan—
money, intimidation, punishment, and other
unpleasant pressures now secure the same end.
To close these rotten boroughs was effectual
enough as far as it wont. To give even a
partial protection in voting by the Ballot, will
be a further step in the same direction. The
Reform of 1832, which was sedition, treason,
felony, and blasphemy to their father's is, as
now continued, as a matter of course, a great
offence to them. The same jingles of accusatory
phrases which the men of the older generation
flung at the heads of their opponents are now
on the lips of the:younger generation of sham
political purists.

Mr. FALB in the recent debate insisted that
the Ballot was only a protection to those who
wanted to tell falsehoods. But were it so, it
seems reasonable enough that impunity for
hypocrisy and false-speech should not be con-
fined to the House of Commons. If an honour-
able member is to have the privilege of deceiving
his constituents by quibbles and pretences,
why not the constituents have an opportunity
of throwing him over by an artifice like his
own? If men rare to cheat each other and
laugh at each other in polities, let all have a
fair chance in the game. The people will not
accept these House of Commons talkers against
the Ballot, as true interpreters of what is un-
manly or un-English. Nor will they confound
phrase-makers, with sound politicians, nor
decriers of secrecy with lovers of truth. The ,
facts of history go farther to settle a question
than the big words of pretentious M.P.'s The '
poor bleeding Galway voters taken to thB poll
by the police under pressure from their land-
lords, pelted with stones through the instiga-
tions of their own priests, are scarcely worth a
thought to our fine manly Englishmen, except
when the adherent of one of our parties is to
be seated or unseated on petition. To be
dragged to the poll by one party, and pelted
and battered with stones by the other is not
pleasant, and can scarcely be considered as a
gratifying exercise of a voter'a independence.
Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE has lofty ideas of
English manliness, but there is little use in
talking about this till it ceases to be a sham.
We admit with him that the Bill is not a good
Bill, but not for the reasons he stated. Bad
as this Bill is, defective in many respects as
we believe it to be, we are very glad that it
has some chance of becoming law, notwith-
standing the flowery protests of its opponents.
Their patriotic) speeches were very good, as
speeches, and their British attitudisiug was
quite graceful; but looked at carefully it can
be seen through, like the trick of those ancient
Italian thieves who went into crowds with
false hands, placed palm to palm on their
breasts pointing to heaven, whilst their real
hands were employed in pioking their neighbours
pockets. That respecter of manhood, STAUNTON'
LYNcri, the Galway Deputy - Lieutenant,
is a real personage, who had PATRICK BUTLERS'
house levelled to the ground because he voted
for the other side, Of course, a voter may be
very manly, and love open voting, though his
house should be pulled down over his head in
consequence. But we should prefer believing
this on his own testimony, rather than on the
word of Sir STAFFORD NORTIICOTE. It will be
difficult, no doubt, to check effeetnally the
aggressive ruffianism of wealth and power, but
we must do our best in this way: that man-
hood may have a chance of maturing in the
poor and dependant, whilst the evil energies
of influential and :powerful persons are under
restraint.

articles.title: RELIGIOUS PERSECUTION IN ROUMANIA.
articles.text:
RELIGIOUS PERSECUTION IN
ROUMANIA.

Tux persecution of the Jews in Roumania
had the effect of bringing together last week in
the City a number of wealthy and highly-
placed persons, amongst others Lord SHAFTES-
BURY and the Bishop of GLOUCESTER, to protest
against its un-Christian character, and to ask
the British Government to interfere for its
prevention. The speeches delivered, wore
moderate enough, and the kind of intervention
asked for was quite in accordance with our
most improved ideas of non-intervention.
We have got beyond such
_a barbarous zeal for
Christianity ourselves. What we at one time
indulged in with revolting cruelty, and an
insatiable instinct for blood, penetrated by a
natural enough desire for plunder, we now
regard with horror. Thanks to the persever-
ance of Liberal men, the Jew is now a free
citizen of the British Empire, and may go
, about his business like other men, safe in
purse and person, without any risk even to his
teeth, which in the olden times ho had too
frequently to part with if he was determined to
keep his money. We know how short the
time is since our Parliament consented to
allow Jews to enter its hallowed precincts,
and we know also now that they are there
how hard it is to recognise any difference
bet ween them and their Christian brethren.

This Jew-hating and Jew-slaughtering is a
very ancimit practice amongst people calling
themselves Christians; and, perhaps, in Eng-
land more than anywhere else, the chosen
people have felt most heavily the hand of the
pious persecutor.

In the reign of STEPlrxrf, that "worthy
peer whose breeches cost him but a crown,"
tha Jews were accused of having cruci-
fied a Christian child at Norwich, to
show their contempt for CuarsT ; and,
although this accusation was utterly false,
it did well enough as a pretext for harry.
ing the children of Israel and laying hands on
their money msst remorselessly. During
HENRY the SECOND'S reign, this stupid charge
was again made as having been committed at
Gloucester. It was, in fact, always repeated
when any horrible cruelty or fraud was
intended; no form of imposition being too
gross to be resorted to by knaves when
ignorant brutal mobs are hounded on to deeds
of cruelty in the name of religion. When this
said HENRY wished to make a voyage to the
Holy Land, he called a Parliament at North-
ampton, and to defray the expenses of his
pious errand, taxed the Jews at £60,000,
though from the whole body of his
.Christian
subjects he only demanded 470,000.
The lion-hearted IticaAnn, whose Holy
wars are read with such pleasure by children,
was a terror and a scourge to the Jews
in England. The great mass of the English,
rich and poet., regarded the Jews as sorcerers,
and hated and feared them; as such. Out of
this came a general massacre in London.
Such a saturnalia of blood has seldom been
seen as that which almost exterminated the
Jews on the occasion of RICHARD'S coronation.
On the eve of a crusade, a stroke of wholesale
Jew-murder was considered rather a good
augury, especially as it usually led to the
picking up of a large sum of money in aid of
the expedition. Who can read without horror
of that heroic, resistance of the Jews in
.York
Castle, where, rather than surrender to the
savage, priest-led mob, into whose hands they
were about to fall, they cut the throats of
their wives and children, and killed each
other after having reduced their treasures to
ashes. Thus the game went on; at one time a
general slaughter, at another an individual
operation, like that performed by order of
King JOHN upon the Bristol Jew, who, because
he declared himself unable to pay the ten
thousand marks of silver demanded, ordered
that he should lose a tooth every day till he
complied. For seven days the poor Jew
submitted, and parted with a tooth a day.
On the eighth, however, he paid the ten
thousand marks, and saved the remainder of
his teeth.

The clergy encouraged this horrid work, but
fla they could not so openly indulge in blood-
letting as laymen, they pursu.ed their perseea -
.ions more in accordance with their professions

of peace, LLNGION, Archbishop
,ef
,Canter-
bury, by the decree of a Synod, orah4tlg that•
no Christian shouldnell provisions to a Jew on
pain of excommunication. Thus the 'thing
went on for years—nay, centuries: Advaiiiing

. WE have been during the last few days into
Somersetshire for the purpose of ascertaining
the real condition of the agricultural laboUrers

of that county.
On entering 11fOntaaub, about five miles
from Yeovil, we were forcibly struck
by the loveliness of the scenery imme-
diately; surrounding the village. The first
object of note is the splendid mansion of the
Pantos family, who are the great landowners
in the district. Montacute House was built
nearly 300 years ago of stone, which is obtain-
able from some excellent quarries now in full
work on .Ham-hill. ' Tlie whole, Or nearly so,
of the houses in the Place aro built of this
particular stone, which is said to excel in
some respects the celebrated Bath stone:
Montacute is situated almost in the extreme
southern portion of the mid-division of Somer-
setshire. The wages have recently been
increased in consequence of the agitation of the
agricultural labourers in different parts of the
country, and are now 10s. a week on the
average possihly a little less. Only a short
time since, however, they were Bs. a-week.
We made a number of inquiries in the houses
of the poor labourere, and elioited the most
paitiftil facts, some of which we give.
A Man, 70 years of age, piece worker, said
he had Is 6d a-day, and a family of ten
persons, ranging in age from 16 downwards.
Some Of the family were able to earn some-
thing towards their maintenance, but had to
de 09 to the total neglect of their education,
which is a deplorable condition of things. The
cottage to, accommodate this family consisted
of three small rooms, for which is. 6d. a-week
is paid as rent.
A labourer earned 193. a-week, raised re-
Candy from 9s. Rent of cottage is. 3d. a-week.
it contiiineetwo rooms only, in one of
which, the bedroom, 13 persons had slept on
some occasions. Two years ago there was no
garden to the cottage. There were six children
iii thelaraily besides the father aud mother.
Some of the children were able to earn a little
in farm work, but not enough to find them
with a s,ufficient quantity of bread, which is
W. the quartern loaf. The wife assured us
tkat the family had not tasted butchers' meat
this year.
We 'visited another family consisting of 10
persons, inolnding the father and mother.
The Wages had been 9s, and were now 10s. a
week. For the cottage is. 6d. a week was
paid. The females of the family, the mother
'and one daught3r, 'eked out the wretched
wages of the father by doing work for the
glove manufacturers. There was a small
piece of allotment ground which grew potatoes
enough to last for about three months in the
year, and for which a rent of Is. a year was
paid.
In some cottages which we visited the
rooms were almost bare of furniture. The
tingle bedrooms, which in many oases had to
accommodate the whole of a family, often
contained nothing but a squalid bedstead, and
'perhaps a small table and a broken chair, with
a few ragged clothes on the bedsteads, not
nearly enough to keep the poor creatures
warm. Clothes, in fact, which would have
been barely sufficient to cover one bed, had to
serve also for the covering of the little ones,
who had to lie about in different parts of the
floor.

Amidst all this terrible poverty of the agri-
cultural labourers in Montacute, the land in
_

the neighbourhood is some of tho richest in the
whole of the county. in fact its productiveness
is so good that a large farmer can realise a
fortune in seven yelrs in Ow district. The
farmers therepay £1 10s. and £2 an acre for
land that is worth £4 and £5 an acre re-
spectively, and the profits on. farming are
consequently enormous, One farm contains
500 acres of land worth about X 4 an acre, but for

which the-farmer, pays about 30s. an acre,
On this farm ten men are only employed. On
another farm of 200 acres two men only are
employed.
It is of course impossible that a man with a
wife'and large family can properly feed and
clothe them on Stich niiserable wages as are
received by farm labourers in Somersetshire.
They do not "live," hi the proper sense of the
ivord. All that Can be Sat& is that "they
don't die." The wages received by the agri-
cultural labourers in Mentaeute mostly repre-
sent their condition, because the keeping of
pigs is the exception and not the rule. Many
people imagine that the resident labourer,
besides .his .wages, almost obtains a living
for his family by keeping a pig.,
This is not so, and, as a proof, we may say
that Mr.. G. NIITCIIFILL, at the meeting on Mon-
day evening, offered to give a sovereign to
each labourer who could drive his pig into
the Square, and he asked the labourers present
that owned a. pig to hold up their hand, but
not one of them did so.

From tho report which we publish in
another column of a meeting held at Monta7
cute on Monday last, it will.be seen that all ,
we have stated has been fully_ confirmed, and
that the condition of the agricultural la-
bowers at Montacute and other parts of
Somersetshire is a disgrace to the nation.
Great credit is due to Mr. G. liftnintr,, who
is a native of that district, and who is
" one from the plough," for promoting a
meeting in his own village, and which pro-
mises such good results to the poor agricul-
tural labourers.

or lock-out. The deputation from the men
opened the proceedings, by saying they ttended
there to support the terms contained in the
memorial sent in s)me weeks since for a working
week Of 51 hours or nine hours per day at 9d. per
hour, with a code of working rules to be mutually
agreed upon, but they were prepared to hear any
proposition from the committee, although they had
no power to refuse or accept such proposition
without having first reported it to the meeting of
delegates. To this the committee replied that they
had not received instructions to- make any pro-
posal whatever, but that the society would meet
again next week. The deputation then stated that
under these circumstances it was no use prolongin g
the interview, as they had no power to secede from
the terms of the memorial. They expressed great
disappointment at being invited to attend the com-
mittee, when it was not intended to make any
proposals for their consideration. The interview
then terminated.

In the evening a meeting of the delegates was
held at the Brown Bear, when a report was given
in of the result of the recent conference between
masters and men respecting the demand of the

latter for the nine hours movement and an increase
of pay. The interview had proved unsatisfactnry ;
and, after a long discussion, the meeting unani-
mously resolved that the men in the employ of
Messrs. Jackson and Shaw, of Pimlico, and of
Messrs. Brass, of Old-street, St. Luke's, should
cease work in accordance with the notice ulready
given, and the men, in ceasing work, placed upon
strike pay. The delegates from the above Arms
stated that the whole of the c.arpenters employed
there would cease work on Saturday ,

Tint STRIKE AT TWO 21.10(1.

On Saturday all the men employed by the firms
of Messrs. Brass, Of 01d-street, St. Luke's, and
Messrs. Jackson and Shaw, of Pimlico, to the
number of about 850, struck work. The men de-
mand that a day's work shall consist of nine hours
(on Saturday six hours), and that the wages shall
be increased to bd. per hour. This rate of pay-
ment will increase their weekly stipend by about
7d. only, and their principal motive in making the
demand is, according to their own account, to give
employment to the unemployed artisans, who at
present form about one-tenth of the trade. The
firms of Messrs. Brass, of St. Luke's, and Jackson
and Shaw, had been singled out, because their
contracts were the heaviest now in progress. The
first has the new Post Office in hand, and the
second firm are responsible for the Home Office at
Whitehall, as well as for the Midland Hotel at
St. Pancras.

MEETING. Or THE DELEGATES.

On Saturday night, the delegates, to the number
of about 200, assembled at the Brown; Bear
Tavern, Bloomsbury, Mr. Sadler in the chair.
Mr. Matkin, the secretary, stated that since the
interview of the deputation with the masters'
committee on the previous Thursday, no further
communication had been receivod from that body,
but he understood they were to meet shortly to
decide upon the course of Action to be adopted.
The delegates from the firms who bad struck on
that day then gave in their morts. The principal
out-door iob of Jackson and Shaw's was the new
Colonial Offices in Downing-street, and that of
Brass's, the new Post Office in St. Martin's-le-
Grand, and at both those places every man had
left.

A discussion then arose as to the propriety of
the men who had come out on strike accepting
work at other firms at the existing hours and
prices, pending the settlement of the dispute; but
such a course was objected to as being unfuir both
to the masters and the men, and a resolution pro-
posed, allowing
,men so to go to work, was nega-
tived by a majority of 90. It was also resolved
to call out the men at the Highgate job of Jackson
and Shaw.

The various delegates then handed in the
amount of the levies paid by their constituents for
the support of the men who had come out, and
which made a large sum in the aggregate. The
remainder of the business consisted of details pre-
paving far the-eventuality oft 10a-Ottt.

MEETING OF Mg MBX O STP.IXE.

On Monday morning the carpenters on strike
met at the Brown Bear, Bloomsbury. The men as
they arrived entered their mimes and addresses,
to the number of over 300, in the strike-book,
which they will have to repeat from time to time
till the struggle terminates, and then ascended to
the club-rootn, a long, low-roofed, and crowded

apartment, where a discussion was going on under
the chairmanship of Mr. Hawkins, Que of tho.

delegates, upon • various matters of detail
requiring prompt decision, In due course
the meeting was regularly opened, and
then delegate communicated " the opinion
of counsel," who desired his name should be with-
held, but not because he had given 'advice

gratis," that picketing was now illegal, and that
if thero was any wish to warn off" from the
closed shops and jobs by •means of placards, the
boards must be borne PA the shoulders of men
who are neither in the trade nor directly concerned,

in the stake, This introduced the very serious
question of " picketting," which wan calmly

arguoil out upon a motion "that , pickots
should be plzioed 'upon any of tho shops or jobs
from which the men luta tamed out." The aup-

porters of this view contended that the object
they were fighting for was toe self-evident, too
intelligible, to need such doubtful aid as pickets,
and indUlging the hope that keeping strictly
within the law, aud relying only upon their own

good cause and just and sound arguments, they
.would insure public support, and act far more
favourably upon the concessional disposition of
their masters. The meeting was very nearly
equally divided upon what' was called "ibis deli-

there were 99 to 97 in favour of an amendment
that pickets be, placed at ell the shops and jobs,
but that the piekete- be allowed s discretion in

result, demanded a poll, which was taken by the
one side returning to a spacious taproom belo',
and the other remaining, when the ,number a were
reversed—there being 109 for the amendment and
, 113 against it, so that the original motion was
carried, and no organized watching wlll be ro7
sorted to. It was also*docidod by a largo majority
that no tuan.out on strike' should seek for or accept
employment at any time 9 the existing terms.

MEETING OF TIIE MASTER. BUILDERS.

The Master Builders' Association has not been
slow to take up the gauntlet thrown down by the
men who have turned out on strike from the shops
and works of Messrs. Brass, Old-street, St Luke's,
and Messrs. Jackson and Shaw, Plaine°, A full
meeting of the committee of the assodation was
held on Monday afternoon at the Freemasowe
Tavern, Great Queen-street, Lincoln's-inn-fields,
and after deliberating with closed doors, for up,
wards of two hours, it was resolved "to convene
, a general meeting of the trade, and to recommend
a general look-out unless the workmen return to
Messrs. Jackson and Shaw, and Mews. Brass on
the existing terms without delay." At the meet-
' lag Mr. Jackson gave an amount of the improve-
ment in wages during the past fifteen years.
Up to 1847, the general rate of pay in the
building trade was ,30s. per week of GO
hours, or Gd. per hour, though the hour
system was not then recognized as such. In
that year the length of the working week was

Last night a special meeting of the Carpenters'
Nine flours Committee was bold for the purpose
of arranging the matters connected with the pay
of the men on strike. All the men belonging to
the General Union, the Amalgamation, or the local
societies will receive the regular strike pay
guaranteed by the ' rules of their respective
societies, but special provision will be made for the
non-society men. It Was reported that although
no:picketing was 'carried on, the committee had
made most effeative anangements for ascertaining
the position of the two firms struck as regards
workmen. No man had gone in, nor had the firms
taken any action to proeure them, but were awaiting
the decision of the masters at the general meeting.
The number of men who have turned out from
the two " teat " firms has been variously atatcd,

on Wednesday intelligence was brought in that a

steps were taken to secure the assistance of an

- THE LONDON VAINTERS.

A delegate meeting of painters was held on
Saturday evening lest at the King's Head, Ebury-
bridge, Pimlico; Mr. George fithipten in the chair.
Resolutions were unanimously adopted for sending
in a memorial to the employers requesting the
concession of nine hours per day, or 61 hours per
week, and that the rate of payment be a minimum
of /id. per hour, the maximum to be fixed by
mutal agreement between the workman and the
employer. An executive committee was appointed
to carry out the movement. Another meeting,
with the same result, was held on Monday night
at the Grey Hound Tavern, Kennington; The
reason why the painters fix the minimum at Sid.
per hour instead of 9d. is that at the present time
their wages are id. per hour less than the men en-

TUU BUIRTOL CLUPENTERS.

On Monday
,evening a meeting of the employers
of carpenters-in the building trade was hold at the
Athenreurn.' Mr. J. Postorpresided, and there was
a limited attendance of employers, numbering about
20. The chairman opened the proceedings by read-
ing a communication he had received on Saturday
from Mr. John Westaway, " the secretary of the
Carpenters and Joiners' Union, to the effect that,
feeling.they were not paid in proportion to many
towns of lesi note and population than this city,
the carpenters and joiners could not accept the offer
made by the employers in the present instance;
but holding that the .principle of arbitration was
just and equitable, they would respectfully submit
this important question to such a tribunal, or, fail-
ing in that, to an umpire, pledging themselves to

The masters having agreed to arbitrate, the
next question was the selection of names from
which the arbitrators should be chosen. The
Chairman suggested Mr. Brice, the Mayor, Mr.
Alderman Abbot, Mr. Alderman Ford and Mr. W.
K. Wait. Mr. Christopher Thomas and Mr. F.
Terrell were named to the list to be sent to the
workmen; and Messrs. Foster, Davey, Banner,
W. Baker, Davis, jun., Coates, Grant, and Kraus
having been appointed a deputation to have an
interview with the men on Monday next, the pro-

TILE HOUSE CARPENTERS OF PRESTON.

A. meeting of the employers of house carpenters
and joiners having been held at the Castle Inn,
Preston, to take into consideration the six months'
notice received from tho workmen to reduce the
working time five hours per week, after some con-
siderable discussion it was decided to accede to
the request of the men, on the ground that they
were asking for no more than the stonemasons,
bricksetters, fiaggers, slaters and plasterers, have
enjoyed.for some time, arid could seo• no reason

THE OPERATIVE PAINTERS OF LEICESTER.

On Saturday last, the operative painters at a
general meeting, held at the Russell Tavern,
Portland-street, unanimously adopted a resolution
to the majority of the masters of the town, thank-
ing them for having conceded to the men the nine
hours movement and alio giving them a slight
advance in wages. The men by this alteration will
work one hour per day less than they have been
doing, and will receive slightly increased pay.

A numerously attended meeting of carpenters
and joiners was held on Thursday evening, in the
preat Albion-street School, at Ha!Mx, for the
purpose of hearing the decision of the employers
on the application of the men for an increase of
their wages from 27g. to 28s. per week, and a re-
duction in the hours of labour from 521 to 50 per
week. The reply of the employers was that they
would grant the reduction of hours, but would not

would expire on Monday at half-past five in the

It was stated that Mr. Joseph Bedforth, of Horton-

The request of the operative stonemasons of
Halifax, for an advance of is. per week in their
wages and an hour's loss work on Saturdays, has
been complied with by the employers, and the now
arrangement will come into operation next Monday.

The working hours of the carpenters and
joiners (and the whole of the operatives in the
building trade) of Gloucester is reduced from 60
to 66i per week at the previous rate of wages,
thereby gaining 311 hours. The men memorialised
for 64, and the employers offered 66i, and the
men returned to work after being out a few days.
The joiners of Tyldesley and Chowbent have
come to an amicable settlement with their em-
ployers, resulting in an advance of 2s. on the
previous rate of wages and 1/ hours less time,
making it 28s. per week of 54 hours, commencing
June lat.

At Sheffield the joiners' strike still continues,
yet each weekly return shows that the men are
gradually gaining ground by individual employers
conceding the demand of the time and wages upon
which the strike originated. During the first week
of the past month there were 55 members of the
society signing the book, in the second week 49,
in the third week 42, and at present the number
is 41.

The joiners' strike at St. lielen's has been
brought to a satisfactory termination, the master
builders having conceded the demands of the
carpenters and joiners for one hour less time and
is. Gd. more wages, which makes the standard

The carpenters of Darwen have succeeded in
obtaining an advano of 2s. per week, after a strike
of nearly one month's duration; their wages will
now be 300. per week for 54 hours.

At Belfast the carpenters have reduced their
working time three i.lolllls a week, commencing
Juno Ist, 51 hours being now the recognised time
to constitute a week's working time.

The joiners' strike at Leicester is virtually ended,
only four members remain on the funds. There
were, at the beginning of May, twenty on the
books, the numbers being reduced to the present
limit by work being obtained on the terms
originally demanded by tho men.

Negotiations being Pending upon the notice
given to the builders,of Lincoln by tho earpoutors
setue time since, it is requested that strangers
abstain frotn seeking work in that, locality until
the wages and thno question is settled.

articles.title: LONDON TAILORS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON TAILORS.

A large meeting of operttive tailors was held
on Tuesday night in the Cambridge Hall, New-
man-street, for the purpose of further organizing
and strengthening the Amalgamated Society of
Tailors, an association formed with a view to bet-
tering the condition of the operatives in the trade,
and of ultimately improving their position with
relation to the masters. The society, though
strongly supported in the country, does not appear
to have succeeded in London, as out of some 20,000
working tailors, only about 800 have become
members.

Mr. G-eorge Potter presided, and was supported
by Mr. Peter Shorrocks, secretary of the Amalga-
mated Society of Tailois ; Mr. Alfred Bailey,
president:; and the committee of the London
branches.

The chairman opened the proceedings in a brief
but suitable speech.

Mr. Shorroeks then addressed the meeting, and
detailed the usefulness and necessity of the society
of which he was the advocate. Nearly fifty
towns had received an advance, varying from 12
per cent. to 25 per cent. whore branches of the
Society existed. They had spent nearly £9,000 in
donations to members, and they wanted to organize
London, and increase the number of' branches.
They had every desire to do their utmost to
attain this object, and ho trusted that at the next
Conference of Tailors, London would be well repre-
sented, and thereby secure some share in the
management.
Mr. W. Cucklan moved the following resolu-
tion :—Resolved—" Having board an explanation
of the rules and principles of the Amalgamated
Socitty of Tailors, and the benefits and advantages
gained by its nretabers and the trade generally
through this Unity, this meeting declares it worthy
the support of the journeymen tailors throughout
the kingdom, and hereby pledge ourselves to pro-
mote the unity of the trade, by every legitimate
and legal moans at our command, that our profes-
sion may hold a position amongst other branches
of industry, honourable and respected by the
pubic generally, useful to all, and a credit to its
members."

Mr. David Desmond seconded the resolution,
which was supported by Mr. Thomas Stokes, Mr.
Reuben Newberry, and carried unanimously.
• Mr. Henry McDonald moved the next resolu-
tion :—Resolved—
" That, inasmuch as the Rxecutive 'Council of
the Amalgamated Society of Tailors have received
power, by votes of its members throughout the
country, to make arrangements with all tailors'
societies to become integral branches or members
of one Association this meeting, called by the
London branches of Society, invite the officers
and members of the London Operative Tailors'
Protective Association to appoint ai committee, to
meet a joint committee of the Loudon branches:of
the above society, for the purpose of placing our
trade in Lcndon and the provinces on an equal
footing with kindred associations."
Mr. James Ellerington having seconded it, Mr.
Alfred Bailey, of Preston, supported the tesolu-
don in a practical speech, in which he showed the
necessity and advantages of unity, and appealed
to the tailors of London to join the Amalgamated
Society without further delay, so that, by their
combined action, they might show to the employ-
ers their dutermination to make another effort to
improve their condition.
Mr. L. Hearn having also supported the resolu-
tion, it v as carried unanimously.
After a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman
for presiding, and for the deep interest he had
long taken in the welfare of working men, one of
the best meetings ever held by the London tailors
terminated.
