THE AGRICULTURAL LAIMMIERS.,

The National Agricultural Labourers' Congrtss,.
was resumed on Thursday morning at Leamington.
Mr. George Dixon, M.P. for Birmingham, again
occupied the chair, and a number of the friends
the movement were on the platform. The 'whole
of the day was occupied in reading papers and
discussion on subjects connected with the welfare
' -
of the working classes.

The chairman read a paper from the UM.
Auberon Herbert, M.P. for Nottingham, dated
from the House of Commons. The hon. gentlemasti
said he hoped the Conference, among other thiPifik
would petition Parliament to remove, as sof* an
possible, aU those mouldy laws which affect the
possession of lind in England, and have no-,
cumulated large properties in few 'hands., Re
condemned primogeniture and the law of entail
and the power to grant long leases. The laws of
England allowed very fanciful and extravagant
powers to landowners, which had this result, that
the land was not dispersed, but was kept from
generation to generation in large masses; and that,:
when land came to be sold, there was difficulti.
and uncertainty in proving to whom it belongedi
and there was the possibility that some one of the
many persons to whom it had been left might re-,
appear some day and claim it. The confusion',
delay, uncertainty, and expense of the present
system were discovered the moment a person
purchased laud, and had to call in a lawyer, who,
like a rabbit in a warren, could alone:find his way
through the labyrinth of legal difficulties which.'
surrounded the question of who is the legal
owner of the land. This entailed a heavy lawyer's'
bill, and ho had been told on good anthority that
the experience of a well-known firm showed that
while the legal coat for large estates was 2i. per
cent., in the case of the smaller estates the
lawyer's bill amounted to £26 per cent. What,
they should require of Parliament was—that
it should leave power to every man who holds
land to sell it, or leave it by will to any person, or,
lease it for any number of years not exceeding the
average term of a man's life after he attains the
age of 21, or to leave it to a great many different
persons in a great many different ways, and under
many different conditions. At. the same time all
parsons interested in land should call upon Parlia-
ment to establish machinery which in some .forns;
or other exists in all other countries in Europe
Every landowner should be compeelled without
delay to register the amount of laud he holds and
to prove his right to it. This once done, whenever
land was bought or sold, there would be no delay,
no expense, and no uncertainity. Then the pur-
chaser would merely have to go with the person
who sold the land to the county office, and it would
be transferred from the vendor to the purchaser.
This might cause some inconvenience and expense
to the present holders of laud, but it might be
done in sueh a manner that in the end they would
, be gainers rather than losers; but the importance
of this step was so great that there ought neither
to be hesitation nor delay in the matter. The
great mass of the English people were separated
from the soil, but, as was the case in France,
Switzerland, and other countries, there was no
reason why English labourers should not be look-
ing forward to saving money for the purchase of
land. There was no reason, even with our system
of large farms, why labourers should not own their
cottages, gardens, or holdings when the present
bad laws are removed and a simple machinery sub-
stituted. He was not in favour of the scheme
sometimes proposed of buying up all the lead and
making it national property. He thought they
could achieve their object by less revolutionary
and fairer means, but they ought not to let the
question rest until the unnatural and fanciful
powers men have to tie it up have been removed,
and registration offices established, so that a man
who bad saved £SO or SO might be able to go to
the county office and claim for himself the first
acre of land that was for sale. At any rate, let
the system which existed in other countries be
tried in England, and see whether some part of
the soil could not find its way into the hands of
a hardworking and thrifty people.
Mr. Taylor, of Leamington, read a paper on
Trades Unionism, and :a resolution was adopted
affirming that it is calculated to improve the
masses of the people, and pledging the Congress to
promote it.
Sir Baldwin Leighton, of Leighton, Salop; next
road a paper Oa meadow and garden allotments for
firm labourers. He argued that the positioa of
labourers might be very greatly improved, without
any sudden Qr great increase of wages, by allowing
them land to culti% ate, which would increase their
incomes, ameliorate tho'r condition, increase their
attachment to the soil, promote contentment, and
eventually exterminate pauperism. He advocated
gardens of at least a quarter of an sera being Atm

tached to each cottage, and said they would be
able to pay a higher rent for the land than the
farmers, lie also urged that, under proper re-
strictions, a further boon might be accorded by the
grant of a few acres of grass land, so as to enable
a ' cow to be kept. Sir Baldwin summed up the
prospective advantages :-1, selection by moans of
thrift of the best labourers, reacting upon the rest
In the general promotion of provident habits; 2,
eloyation of the individual labourer and the whole
faiily,by increased self-respect and carefulness,
and 'increased income depending on the carefulness;
3, supplementing of wages by the labourer's own
exertions at
,no perceptible cost to landlord or
farmer; 4, comparative contentment and comfort,
with a strong attachment to a place of labour; 5,
gradual extinction of pauperism and improvidence,
including drunkenness. From experience gained
in this way, great good might follow in opening
a way and a prospect ti the best men to rise. lle
thought 'it possible, also, to introduce industrial
partnerships into agriculture, by giving extra pay-
multi, in addition to weekly wages, on theprineiple
which was adopted with regard to shepherds for
rearing the greatest number of lambs.

Mr. Stretten, Mr. Strange, the Rev. Mr. Pigot
(Edgmont Rectory, Salop), and others spoke in
favour of the proposals advanced by Sir Baldwin
Leighton, and the following resolution was
adopted
"That it is desirable, as much in the interest of
employers as of thoso employed in agriculture,
that the labourer should have some greater interest
in the soil by way of garden allotments and cow
land., or otherwise."
The meeting then adjourned, and on again
assembling, Mr. Jesse Collings,' of Birmingham,
read a paper on education as a means of amelio-
rating the condition of 'farm labourers lie spoke
of the value and importance of education, and
urged" the 'working men of England to, vote for
compulsory education and to insist On the election
of School Boards in 'every parish.
The Chairman called special attention to a
resolution submitted, affirming that, in the opinion
of the Conference, a national compulsory system
of education is absolutely necessary for advancing
the social condition of agricultural labourers. lie
said there was doubt among persons in high
positions whether labourers desired a system of
national education, and if so, whether it should be
compulsory. lie asked those delegates who were
able to express the views of labourers in their
district, either by voting for or against the reso-
lution, ad asked thou) who felt they could not do
so to remain neutral. He said he should attach
importance to this resolution, and should refer
to the decisiou of the Conference in the House of
Commone, becnnse hitherto there had been no
opportunity of eliciting the opinions of agricul-
turists on this subject.

The Rev. Artbur O'Neill, of Birmingham, ob-
jected to extraneous questions being introduced,
and said that if any attempt was made to use the
decision of the Conference in any way, he should.
feel it his duty to say it was adopted hurriedly,
and after very immature consideration.
After some farther discussion the resolution was
ad 01404, only R. ciyv. deputies voting against it.
The- Hon.
,r 4411 Rev. W. Leigh, rector of
Stoneleigh,,and brother of the Lord-Lieuteuant of
the county, read a paper on co-operative agricul-
ture. He referred to tiro attempts made by Mr.
Scott Vandeleur at Ralahine, county Clare, in
1830, and the experience of the Assington Co-
operative Agricultural Society, in Suffolk, ori-
ginated by Mr. Guerdon, in 1830. He suggested
that landlords with home farms might make the
experiment of co.operative farming, on the Rala-
bine system; that large tenant farmers might do
the same thing on the partnership principle,
adopted with such success by Mr. Briggs's colliery
and Messrs. Crossley, of Halifax; that a society
might be formed in London to reclaim and culti-
vate wastelands ; and that where a co-operative
store exists, efforts should be made to procure a
small farm and dispose of portions of the proceeds
at the store.

After some discussion, a resolution was adopted
that, in the opinion of that Conference, co-opera-
tive farming may become a powerful means by
which the condition of the agricultural labourer
may be improved, and a greater interest given
bun in the cultivation of the soil.

Mr. henry Brooks, of London, read a paper in
favour of the cultivation of waste lands and small
farms by agricultural labourers, and quoted
statistics to show this could be beneficially and
profitably done.
A resolution was adopted declaring that the
Enclosure Commission should be abolished, and
that enclosures should be in future effected by a
Board of Reclamation, to be constituted by Parlia-
ment, for, the purpose of beteg cliyided into smell

farms, to be sold or leased to small farmers and
agricultural labourers.
Mr. Hemming, the Staffordshire delegate,
condemned the Game Laws, and urged the import-
ance of agricultural labourers agitating for the
franchise, but, at the suggestion of the chairman,
ho abstained from moving any resolution on these
subjects, though the mention. pf them elicited
enthusiastic cheering.

Mr. Dixon, in acknowledging a vote of thanks
for presiding, said the agricultural labourers had
set rolling a stone which would not atop until
they had obtained what they believssi to be their
due. It wa.s absolutely certain they would gain
what they called their rights. He counselled
them, as his parting advice, to use discreetly the
increased power they were about to obtain, and
not to attempt to intimidate or cooroo any fellow-
labourer who stood aloof frorn.tho .Union, or to
take advantage in any Way., of employers, as
either one or the Other kind of conduct would
retard the realisation of their desires.
The Conference then ended. •

articles.title: GREAT MEETING AT MONLACUTE.
articles.text:
GREAT MEETING AT MONLACUTE.

For some days past the village of Montacute
has been placarded with bills drawing attention to
"the low wages of the labourers," and last week a
bill was circulated, intimating that a meeting was
to be . held on Monday evening, when Mr. U.
Potter and others would deliver itachessos. Of
course this caused considerable excitement. Mr.
George Mitchell, marble mason; of London,
formerly a labourer at Montacute, but who has
been fortunate in business, knowing the wages at
Montacute, had expressed himself anxious that the
labourers should take advantage of the prevailing
agitation to get an increase.

—Towards the hour fixed for the meeting, men
walked into the village from all directions, and
considerable interest appeared to be taken in the
proceedings. A platform was erected in the Square
The audience was principally composed of labourin g
men, who were exceedingly orderly throughbut,
and patiently listened to every speaker. • There
could not have been less than 1,500 persons pre-
sent.

Mr. George Potter presided, and opened the
proceedings in a speech admirably adapted to the
occasion, and which apparently seemed to give
great encouragement to the labourers present.

The Chairman then said :—" The six members
of Parliament for the county have been . written
to, and five—Mr. Richard Bright, Mr. Gore Lang-
ton, Mr. Neville-Grenville, Major Paget, and the
Ilom. Capt. hood—have written letters of apology
for not being able to attend. There is one para.
graph in Major Paget's letter, which Iwill read to
you.—" The social condition of the farm labourers
may fairly be expected to improve in as rapid a ratio
as that of other industrial classes." Lord Edmund
Fitzmaurice, who has great interest in the ques-
tion, would have been here, but his Parliamentary
clutics prevent his doing so. He, however, wishes.
you" God speed." Professor Fawcett, who is also
much interested in the question, writes, "I most
heartily sympathise with the wise and self-reliant
efforts which the, labouring classes are making on
the soil to better their lot." We should- have had
-
a minister, not of the Church of England—the Rev.
Charles Spurgeon—here,but he has not yet had tinae
to givq the question his attention. Ile writes—"
am so sorely pushed for time that I cannot give, due.
attention to this agricultural question. Where poor.
men are getting only Os., 10s., 1 is., or 123. a week
it ia time that hy some. means they should begin to
advance. I wish the poor agricultural labourers
a speedy deliverance from the laud of bondage."
(Cheers.)
The Chairman called upon Mr. G. Mitchell,
alias "One from the Plough," to aldress the
meeting.
Mr. George Mitchell was received with cheers.
His object in coming there was not, as it had boon
asserted, to spread strife or to sow the seeds of
discord. Montacuto men were as good as York.
ahiremen, and as honest as any class in the
country. He had been introduced to them as one
from the plough, and if anyone would stand up and
say that he was not from the plough ho would
challenge, at the end of a wing), to plough any
farmer in Montaeute for .£5O, the winners to give
the amount to the poor c'f Montacute. (Cheers.)
He saw in front of him several companions with
whom he used to plough, although he wished that
they had a little more "grub." (Laughter.) A
few potatoes and a drop of bane fat once in a day
was not sufficient for any man. (Laughter, cheers,
and voices "That's true.") It waa not sufficient
furs woman. At any rata it was not sufficient for
sotueboiy he know. (Renewed laughter.) He
came down there not to set them striking—that
waa not his object. Some of them struck the other
day. They knew what he said to them.-7" Return
to ,your work." If the farmers. rodueed ,their

wages to 6s. a week, ho would still counsel them
to continue work, because in the meantime they,
could agitate. Would they be surprised to bear
that poor Todd Mitchell, who was literally starved
out of the place 25 or 26 years ago, was now inde-
pendent of the Montacute farmers ? Let thorn
reason the subject with the farmers, who must see
the force of the arguments used. They au not
get boar steaks every day, nor griziled mutton
chops. They had the grizzle—the mutton chops
other people had. Many persons know that he
once earned his living at. the plough's tail. (A
voice—" Yes, and shirt hanging out.", Laughter.),
You do not know the brogue of: Montacute yet.
You ought to have said, "Your butter clout hang-
ing out." (Rtnewed laughter.) Mr. Mitchell then
detailed the history of his life previous to leaving
ktontacute. Ho described the way in which he
measured the ground previous to ploughing. -On
one occasion his master ordered him to -harrow a
field of turnips. He got up at feur in the morn-
ing, harrowed the field, and then loaded hay
uutil tea o'clock at night.. -Ho . bad.. not
had a pennyworth of victuals-ts !sat during the
day, anl at ten o'clock he rested for a time on a
" pook " of hay near the rick. His master saw
him, called him, a lazy fellow, and atternPted to
kick him. He avoided the blow and went home.
On the following Saturday ho gave his master
notice to leave. He was then receiving 4s. a week.
At the end of the fortnight his master increased
his wages t0..55. a week and asked him if he intended
to leave. Mr. Mitchell told him that he did, and
that the 2s. 'extra ho had paid him would be spent
hi leather to carry him away from Abbey Farm.'
His toaster told him that ho would be gl id to go
back again in a month. But the month was • not
yet up.. Mr. Mitchell said that the first new suit
of .clothes he had was mule out of his father's old
Ham Hill trowaers. Mr. Mitchell reminded- the
labourers that they had not long had Bs. a week.
He remembered when the standing wages were
7s. a'week, and When. an attempt was made to re-
duce them to 6r. The occupier pf Abbey Farm
wished to make that.reduction. But the labourers
• would not have it, and the Vs. were continued.
Since this agitation in the north of England he bad
heard that 145., 16.5., and 18s. a week were paid,
and he felt for his poor brethren in Montacute. He
heartily thanked the proprietor of Pubnan's Weekly
Ne re s for the opportunity presented to him of help-
ing the labourers of Montacute. 'He saw a letter
in that paper showing the balance sheet of a
labourer, and •he thought that he 'Could make
something of it. The letter- was headed " The
Devonshire Labourer," and it referral to a labourer
living not a hundred miles from Azininster.-: He
added the ;words "-Somerset, and not 100 'miles
from Yeovil." He then hadialetter printed on a
poster, and these "Brampton sensationals," as they
were termed, were sent to all parts, of the
country. It was stated that labourers had
privileges, and were enabled to keep pigs. He
. would give Ll t 3 every labourer who could
show him a pig which was fed in his own stye
L'Alr. Mitchell asked those who .bad pigs to hold
, up their bands in order that he might fulfil his
, promise—but net one hand was held up.] He had
tray.elled .upon the Continent, and had made
inquiries as to the - wages of the agricultural
labourers—partieularly in 'France, Holland, and
Belgium. The wages ranged from 10s. to its. a
,week, with a house tO live-in rent free. Labourers
. were divided into three classes carters and
shepherds receiving 15s. and 16s. a week. England
was the richest country in the world, and yet the
labourers had only lately been receiving 'Os. and
10s. a week. And had it not been for the
" Bronapton sensationals " he did not believe that
the farmers would even then have increased their
wages. He urged the men 'to join the union for
their. own benefit.

Mr. Mitchell than called upon
Jack llann,.alias Jack Tucker, a very old man,
who, in answer to a question, said that he remain.
bored when his master tried to reduce his wages to
Cs. a week. But he would not accept of it. He
was the forehook" (first Man) for more than
20 years. In harvest time, when he worked from
six o'clock in the nalrning until nine at night, he
could not make More than 10s, or 12s. a week.
He could not now do a day's work, lie received
is. Od. a week and a loaf of bread from the parish,
and if he could got a little work to do he did it.
Mr. Mitchell—And do you pay house rent ?

Tucker—l have not paid anything since Christ-
mas. I cannot afford it.

Win. Chant, an elderlyilabourer, was also called
upon the platform and examined by Mr. Mitchell.
110 said that when be was married he received 10s.
a week. But he worked at Montecute House, and
thin were no perquisites: Varm labourere were
paid 98. a week liad had eight children, and
paid la, tid, week rent. (4.--liow much butcher's

meat did you have? A.—l did not
.eat threepenny-
worth of beef in a twelvemonth.

Amelia Bull, a respectable looking woman, was.
called upon the platform and said that she had had
1:5 children. Q.—How much did your husband
get a week? A.-7s. when we were first married.
Q.—l suppose his wages were increased. to Bs.?
A.—Yes. Q.—His wages have been lately raised
to 98. ? A.—lle has got is. extra. Q.—l sup.
pose you have plenty of butcher's meat?. A.—
None whatever. Q.—Do you pay house rent ?
A.-Is. Gd. a week.

Mr. Mitchell said that he thought he had pio-
dirced sufficient evidence •to convince, every one
that something ought to be clone,for the labourers.
Ile hoped they would become members of the
union. (Cheers.) •
Jacob Bull then moved the following resolution,
which was read by the chairman, the proposer not
being able to read :
" Resolved, that this meeting deeply sympathises
with the long depressed condition of the agricul-
tural 1 rbourers of Somerset arid approves of the
establishment of a branch of the National Agri-
cultural Labourers' Union at Dlontacute, for the
purpose of improving the condition of the labourer.
Anti the Libourers present pledge themselves to be-
come members of the union and to use every effart
to induce other labourers to do likewise."
(Cheers.)

George Hunt seconded , the resolution. Ho
worked front six o'clock in the evening until
twelve at night extra without complaint. At last
he asked for some remuneration for the extra
work, when his master replied that he ought to
have spoken to him before, and refused his appli-
cation. (Cries of "- Shaine.") -
Alfred , Martin supported the resolution. He
said that ha was an agricultural labourer from the
County of Dorset—his home being Milhorne St.
Andrew. His wages were 9s. a week, and the
labourers in his part had long been speaking about
a rise. He had been accustomed to read the
newspapers and noticed the agitation in, Warwick-
shire. He spoke to his fellow labourers, and told
them that they must do something in Dorset.
A branch had been formed at Milborne St.
Andrew and three others had been formed in the
neighbourhood. There was also a desire manifested
for the formation of other branches. Ho be-
lieved that there would be as good a union in
Dorsetshire as there was in Warwickshire. Ho
thought also that there would be a good one in
Somerset. The enrolling of their names would
cost 6d. and a payment of 2d. a week would
ensure 12s, a week at least. •

George Allington, from the Warwickshire
Labourers' Union, also spoke. He noed not multiply
words to prove to them the deplorable condition of
the labouring classes., There were many who did
not and could not have the nocessaries of life.
His business now was chiefly to ascertain the con-
dition in which the agricultural labourer was
found. Ire had investigated the qUestion, and was
convinced that many of them had not bread enough
to eat.

Thomas Harris, a Warwickshire delegate, also
addressed the assembly. Farmers considered the
-labourers' strike as something wonderful. They
:were frightened that the labourers could not live
upon Os: a week, and were surprised at their being
so discontented.. Farmers and others, 'contended
that Os. a week was stitileient. Ile had been
trying to prove that that was net enough, and
he did so in this way. An average family con.
sisted of a man, his wife, and three -children.
They could not allow the family less than three
meals a day, and one penny each meal for each
person. That would make sd. a meal—ls. 3d.
a day, and 83. 9d. a week. If that was considered
too much, he should like any gentleman to tell him
how it could be done for leas. 'He should like to
know what kind of a mutton chop or beef steak a

butcher would cut for a penny. (Laughter.)
There were other things wanted in cottages, such
as cotton, starch, soap, - and these
he considered could not be estimated at
loss than Od„ a week. That mario Os. 6d.
—more than the Montacute labourers received.
They must have boots to walk with, and no shoe-
maker would undertake to keep a family of five in
boots for less than Is. a week. The family would
want clothes, and, Is. a week was not too large an
estimate for that necessity of life. They must
have cottages. But some of them were mere
hovels. Their masters •put their nags into better
places then- the. labourers had to lire in. The
average rent of Is. 6d.- was generally paid in
Somerset. They wanted- light and firing, which
could not be purchased for less than Is. a week.
Instead of Os. or las.- a week, 16s. would not be
found too much for a labourer. (Cheers).
The resolution was put to the meeting and
carried unanimously, amid much thee ri n.
The .Chuitnien il that eta meeting held that
afternoon two trustees, a 'chairman, and a- secre
tary, had been erpointeil relent', atom of the

f
branch. lYfr. H. Hallett and Mr. George Mitchell
were the trustees, Mr. W. noticey was the chair-
man, and Mr. William Drew, secretary. They
now only wanted the names to be enrolled. Those
whose dames could not be enrolled that evening
would be taken on another evening.
The Rev. Silas Walmsley proposed a vote of
thanks to the chairman, to the reporters, and to
Mr. George Mitchell, Vfo had got up the meeting.
He wished the union every success, and may God,
who was a God of justice, help the right and•
defend the noble.

• Mr. WA!. Drew seconded the resolution, and
ekpressed a hope that a largo number would give
in their names as members of the union.
The Chairman briefly returned thanks on behalf
of all concerned, and called for cheers which were
heartily given.
A large number of labourers afterwards entered
their names as members and paid the required
entrande fee.

articles.title: RAILWAY SERVANTS.
articles.text:
THE RAILWAY SERVANTS.

On Sunday afternoon a meeting, composed of
about 800 ernployds of the London and North.
Western Railway Company, including deputy
and sub-foremen, checkers, callers-off, porters,
head-shunters, horse-driers, breaksmen, shippers,
loaders, capstan-men, ice., was held in Milton-hall,
Hawley-crescent, Camden-to wn,to consider the best
stops to be taken by the men in the present un-
friendly relations between them and the railway
authorities. The hall was closely packed by the
men, and 200 or 300 could not obtain admission.
The proceedings were of an excited character.
The chair was taken by Mr. George Chapman,
and subsequently by Mr. J. Baxter Langley.
Mr. Boon (shipper) reminded the meeting that
a memorial bad been sent to the directors of the
company, asking for an increase of wages, averag-
ing from 2s, Od. to as, per week, and other advan-
tages, for checkers, callers-off, head-shunters,
breaksmen, horse-drivers, and porters, on the
ground that " the increased price of animal food,
clothing, and the great advance in house-rent
combined, render the present rate of wages paid to
the memorialists totally inadequate to meet the
wants of themselves and their respective families."
Mr. Greenish, the London superintendent, had
done all he could to stamp out the movement, and
a man named Tarbox, who had been eighteen
years in the company's service as capstan-man,
was dismissed because be took the chair at one of
the meetings. He (Mr. Boon) was told by Mr.
Gil Hard, station-master at Broad-street, that he
was to be paid a fortnight's wages and discharged
for taking the chair at one of the meetings. He
told the station-master that if he were dismissed
there would not be, in one hour, a man to do the
work of the company's station in London. (Loud
cheers.) The result was, he was told to go to his
'work. Mr. Finlay, general goods manager, had
promised that he would lay the memorial of the
men before the directors, and give them an
answer at the end of the ensuing week, and that
he would also bring the case of Tarbox, the dis-
missed man, before the directors, and he was sure
